_note: How-tos are short summaries in my own words; follow the source link for the teacher's full instruction.

practices.name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
practices.howto: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

practices.name: Video lectio (short contemplative reading)
practices.howto: Watch a short image or text slowly, then sit with a single phrase that stays with you before meditating.

practices.name: Centering Prayer
practices.howto: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

practices.name: Welcoming Practice
practices.howto: When a strong reaction arises, feel it as a sensation in the body; say "welcome" to it instead of resisting; then let go of the desire for security, approval or control, and so release it into presence.

practices.name: Lectio Divina
practices.howto: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

practices.name: The Jesus Prayer (prayer of the heart)
practices.howto: Repeat "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me" slowly and attentively, often with a prayer rope, keeping the mind in the words and letting it descend into the heart. Begin with a fixed time each day; humility and stillness come before technique.

practices.name: Zikr (remembrance) in the Inayati way
practices.howto: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

practices.name: Dhikr and breathwork
practices.howto: Join a short divine name or phrase to the in- and out-breath; keep attention on the heart; finish with silence and a prayer.

practices.name: Khatm-i Khwajagan (Naqshbandi group dhikr)
practices.howto: A set Naqshbandi litany of Qur'an recitation, blessings on the Prophet and silent or vocal remembrance, recited together under a shaykh's guidance.

practices.name: Neoplatonic contemplation ("strip away everything")
practices.howto: Following Plotinus, turn attention from objects to the activity of knowing, then let even that subtle self-image fall away, resting in the simple presence it comes from. Usually practised after a period of calming meditation.

practices.name: The view from above (spiritual exercise)
practices.howto: In imagination, rise above your situation until your concerns appear in the scale of the cosmos; return with a lighter, more just sense of what matters. One of the ancient "spiritual exercises" Pierre Hadot described.

practices.name: Hermetic ascent and rebirth (Corpus Hermeticum XIII)
practices.howto: Read slowly and as contemplation, not just as information: the treatise guides the reader to put away the "torments" of matter and be reborn as the intellect praising God in silence.

practices.name: Active imagination / imaginal attention
practices.howto: Stay with an image (from a dream, a text or a place) as a living presence; let it speak and move; respond to it honestly rather than interpreting it away. In Corbin's terms it is a perception of the mundus imaginalis.

practices.name: Weekly parashah reflection (neo-Hasidic)
practices.howto: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

practices.name: Letter-combination meditation (ecstatic Kabbalah)
practices.howto: Abulafia's path: combine and permute the Hebrew letters of divine names, with breath and pronunciation, to loosen ordinary thinking. Historically taught only under a teacher. Listed here for context, not as instruction.
